```{python}
import sys
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
from pathlib import Path

REPO_ROOT = Path("../..")
sys.path.insert(0, str(REPO_ROOT.resolve()))

FIG_DIR = Path("../../figures/03-26-26")
FIG_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

RESULTS = REPO_ROOT / "results"

MODEL_LABELS = {
    "model_simple_contagion":                  "SC",
    "model_complex_contagion":                 "CC",
    "non_parametric_monotonic_empirical_bayes": "NP",
}
MODEL_ORDER   = ["SC", "CC", "NP"]
MODEL_COLORS  = {"SC": "#4C72B0", "CC": "#DD8452", "NP": "#55A868"}
MODEL_MARKERS = {"SC": "o",       "CC": "s",       "NP": "^"}
K_VALUES = [1, 2, 3]
```

```{python}
#| label: helpers
#| warning: false
#| output: false
def load_dir(dataset_name: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    base = RESULTS / dataset_name
    rows = []
    for mc_path in sorted(base.rglob("model_comparison.parquet")):
        sf_dir  = mc_path.parent
        k_dir   = sf_dir.parent
        sf_name = sf_dir.name.replace("stan_file~", "")
        label   = MODEL_LABELS.get(sf_name, sf_name[:12])
        try:
            k_fit = int(k_dir.name.replace("K~", ""))
        except ValueError:
            continue
        df = pd.read_parquet(mc_path)
        r  = dict(df.iloc[0])
        r["K_fit"] = k_fit
        r["model"] = label

        # Pull R-hat / ESS from inference_summary if present
        summary_path = sf_dir / "inference_summary.parquet"
        if summary_path.exists():
            try:
                s = pd.read_parquet(summary_path)
                rhat_col = [c for c in s.columns if "r_hat" in c.lower() or "rhat" in c.lower()]
                ess_col  = [c for c in s.columns if "ess_bulk" in c.lower() or c.lower() == "ess"]
                if rhat_col:
                    r["max_rhat"] = float(s[rhat_col[0]].dropna().max())
                if ess_col:
                    r["min_ess"]  = float(s[ess_col[0]].dropna().min())
            except Exception:
                pass
        rows.append(r)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def load_synth(k_true: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Merge v1 K_fit=1 with v2 K_fit=2,3 for K_true=2,3."""
    if k_true == 1:
        return load_dir("synth_model_sel_k1_20260325")
    v1 = load_dir(f"synth_model_sel_k{k_true}_20260325")
    v1 = v1[v1.K_fit == 1].copy()
    v2 = load_dir(f"synth_model_sel_k{k_true}_v2_20260325")
    v2 = v2[v2.K_fit.isin([2, 3])].copy()
    return pd.concat([v1, v2], ignore_index=True)


def build_waic_pivot(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    return (
        df.pivot_table(index="model", columns="K_fit", values="waic", aggfunc="first")
        .reindex(index=MODEL_ORDER, columns=K_VALUES)
    )


def waic_table(df: pd.DataFrame, cols=("waic", "lppd", "p_waic", "median_log_lik", "max_rhat", "min_ess")) -> pd.DataFrame:
    keep = [c for c in cols if c in df.columns]
    out = df[["model", "K_fit"] + keep].copy()
    out = out.sort_values(["model", "K_fit"]).reset_index(drop=True)
    return out
```

## The Hazard Model

Everything in this project is built on a discrete-time hazard. The basic object is $h(k)$: the probability that a susceptible node adopts in a given time step, given that exactly $k$ of its neighbors have already adopted. This is the **infection kernel**. The whole inference problem is recovering $h(\cdot)$ from observed cascades.

### Full-population survival vs adopters-only

Before getting into the mechanics, it's worth being precise about what estimand we're targeting. There are two natural choices, and they answer different questions.

**Full-population survival** -- the current setup for both OO and Twitter -- includes every susceptible node in the likelihood, whether they ever adopt or not. A node that is exposed to $k=5$ infected neighbors for 100 periods without ever adopting contributes 100 non-event entries at $k=5$ to $N$. This estimates the population-average per-period hazard:

$$h(k) = P(\text{adopt at step } t \mid \text{susceptible at step } t, \ k \text{ infected neighbors at step } t)$$

The denominator is all susceptible nodes at all time steps. Non-adopters are a real part of the denominator.

**Adopters-only survival** filters the dataset to nodes that eventually adopt before building the Stan matrices. Non-adopters are dropped entirely. This estimates a conditional hazard:

$$h_\text{adopters}(k) = P(\text{adopt at step } t \mid \text{will eventually adopt}, \ k \text{ infected neighbors at step } t)$$

This is structurally similar to a case-only likelihood in survival analysis -- you condition on the case occurring and ask about the timing and exposure pattern.

**Why adopters-only might be the right thing to do:**

Many susceptible nodes in real-world data are structurally non-susceptible -- Twitter users who never retweet anything regardless of social pressure, OO players who simply stopped playing. Including them in the full-population hazard pollutes the $N$ counts with observations from nodes that were never going to adopt regardless of exposure level. Their at-risk intervals pull $h(k)$ toward zero at all levels, which is why the Twitter SC/CC fits land at $h(k) \sim 0.003\%$. The NP model partially escapes this because the empirical Bayes prior anchors it to the actual adoption rate.

In the adopters-only frame, structural non-adopters are removed before inference. What remains is the hazard conditional on being a "true susceptible." This is arguably the more interpretable object for understanding social contagion: among the nodes that could be infected by the cascade, what is the shape of their infection kernel?

**Why full-population has advantages too:**

The population-level spread dynamics -- how fast a cascade grows, how large it gets -- depend on the full-population hazard, not the conditional hazard. Adopters-only gives a systematically upward-biased estimate of the kernel because you are conditioning on the outcome. For predicting epidemic size or computing $R_0$, you want the full-population version.

There's also a circularity risk: you define "true susceptibles" as nodes that adopted, then estimate a hazard conditional on having adopted. This makes the kernel look more potent than it is.

**What to expect when re-running adopters-only:**

For Twitter, the NP vs SC/CC gap should shrink. The 1800-unit WAIC gap is partly driven by the mass of non-adopting users whose flat non-event histories force SC/CC to very low rates. With those users removed, all three models estimate a hazard over the same eventually-adopting users, and the kernel shape differences become more about shape than scale. The NP advantage may persist -- the Twitter kernel may genuinely not be sigmoid -- but the magnitude will likely be smaller.

For OO, the simulation generates adoption by the infection kernel with no structural non-susceptibles. Every non-adopting node failed to adopt due to stochastic exposure, not resistance. Adopters-only will remove those "unlucky" nodes and shift estimates upward. The K=3 structure may or may not survive -- it depends on whether the three components reflect genuine subpopulation heterogeneity or the mixing of adopters and non-adopters at different exposure tails.

---

### Data encoding: M and N matrices

For each node $i$ and exposure level $k$, the data is summarized into two counts:

- $M_{ik}$: number of time periods node $i$ spent at exposure level $k$ **and adopted** during that period.
- $N_{ik}$: number of time periods node $i$ spent at exposure level $k$ **and did not adopt**.

Each period at exposure $k$ is an independent Bernoulli trial with success probability $h(k)$. So the likelihood is just a product of Bernoullis across all $(i, k)$ cells:

$$
\mathcal{L}(h) = \prod_i \prod_k \, h(k)^{M_{ik}} \cdot (1 - h(k))^{N_{ik}}
$$

This is a pooled binomial likelihood: all nodes with the same exposure count $k$ share the same $h(k)$ estimate. The Stan data matrices are exactly this -- two 2D arrays indexed by node and exposure level.

### Survival framing

"Survival" here means we track each node's full exposure trajectory over time, not just whether it ever adopted. A node that spent 3 periods at $k=2$, then 2 periods at $k=5$, then adopted at $k=5$, contributes $(1-h(2))^3 \cdot (1-h(5))^1 \cdot h(5)$ to the likelihood. The "survival" part is all those non-event periods accumulating in the denominator.

This is contrasted with a simpler incidence encoding where you'd only record the exposure level at the moment of adoption, discarding the time-at-risk information. Survival uses the full trajectory and is more efficient.

For Twitter specifically (`twitter_mn_mode: "survival"`), the cascade data records each user's exposure level at each time step, so we can build the full M/N matrices. The `V_max_local=1000` cap means we subsample 1000 susceptible nodes per Stan call to keep runtimes tractable.

### Kernel families

The three models differ in what functional form they assume for $h(k)$:

**SC (Simple/Geometric):** $h(k) = 1 - (1 - \rho)^k$. This is the probability of at least one "successful contact" in $k$ independent Bernoulli trials with rate $\rho$. It's monotone, starts near 0, and asymptotes to 1. One free parameter per component.

**CC (Complex/Sigmoid):** $h(k) = \rho_l + (\rho_h - \rho_l) \cdot \sigma(w(k - k_0))$ where $\sigma$ is the logistic function. This allows a threshold-like shape -- near-zero adoption at low exposure, then a steep rise, then saturation. Four free parameters per component: floor $\rho_l$, ceiling $\rho_h$, slope $w$, inflection $k_0$.

**NP (Non-Parametric):** $h(k) = \text{logistic}(\mu_k)$ with a free $\mu_k$ for each exposure level $k = 1, \ldots, k_\text{max}$. No assumed shape. The prior on $\mu_k$ is $\text{Normal}(\mu_0, \sigma)$ where $\mu_0$ is set from the empirical adoption rate (empirical Bayes). $k_\text{max}$ free parameters per component.

### Mixture model

For $K > 1$ components, each node is assumed to draw from a latent population of $K$ susceptibility types with mixing weights $\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_K$. The marginal likelihood for node $i$ integrates over its type assignment:

$$
p(\text{data}_i \mid h_1, \ldots, h_K, \pi) = \sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j \prod_k h_j(k)^{M_{ik}} (1 - h_j(k))^{N_{ik}}
$$

This is a standard finite mixture of Bernoullis. The $K=1$ model is just the single-component case. WAIC is computed from the per-node log-likelihoods $\log p(\text{data}_i \mid \cdot)$ marginalized over type -- so it's valid even when individual chain samples have label-switched component assignments, because the marginal is invariant to permutation.

### Why NP dominates on Twitter

For OO, CC wins: the infection kernel looks like a sigmoid threshold. For Twitter, NP K=1 is ~1800 WAIC units below CC K=1. Now that we have the actual posterior kernel estimates, the reason is concrete.

The NP model estimates Twitter hazard rates of $h(1) \approx 0.8\%$ rising to $h(50) \approx 10.5\%$. The SC model estimates $h(1) \approx 0.003\%$ rising to $h(50) \approx 0.13\%$. The CC model is similar: $h(1) \approx 0.005\%$ to $h(50) \approx 0.03\%$. That's a **100-300x scale difference**. The NP model is not finding a different shape -- it's finding a kernel that lives in a completely different magnitude regime.

The shape itself is monotonically increasing and roughly linear in the NP fit, so the issue is not non-monotonicity or a step function. The problem is that SC and CC are constrained parametric forms that get anchored to very low rates by the mass of non-adoption periods at low exposure, then can't simultaneously explain why nodes DO adopt at high exposure. The SC geometric form $h(k)=1-(1-\rho)^k$ has a single rate parameter $\rho$ -- it can't be simultaneously small at $k=1$ and large at $k=20$. So $\rho$ is pulled toward a compromise that systematically underpredicts adoption events everywhere. The CC sigmoid has more flexibility (four parameters), but still saturates at a ceiling $\rho_h$ that the fit pushes very low.

NP sidesteps this entirely: each $\mu_k$ is independent. The data at $k=20$ directly determines $h(20)$ without being pulled down by data at $k=1$.

Once K=2 and K=3 land for Twitter, SC/CC mixtures can in principle cover multiple scale regimes with different components. But a 1800-unit gap reflects a structural constraint on every individual component's functional form, not just the mixture weights. Even the best-fitting CC sigmoid can't place $h(k)$ in the 1-10% range without also predicting unsustainably high adoption at low exposure. Multiple CC components won't close a 1800-unit gap.

## Synthetic Validation

Before looking at empirical results: do WAIC and bic_median correctly identify K_true?
Synthetic data generated by CC model. K_fit=1 from v1 (1 chain/500/500); K_fit=2,3 from v2
(4 chains/1000/1000).

```{python}
#| label: fig-synth
#| fig-cap: "WAIC vs K_fit for synthetic CC-generated data at K_true=1, 2, 3. Dashed vertical line marks the true K. CC correctly selects K_true=1 and K_true=2 with clear margins. K_true=3 margin is narrow (CC K=3 wins by ~2 units over NP K=2), accepted as a known limitation. 4 chains / 1000 warmup / 1000 samples for K=2,3."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4))
fig.suptitle(
    "Synthetic model selection validation -- WAIC vs K_fit\n"
    "(CC-generated data; dashed line = K_true)",
    fontsize=11,
)

for ax, (k_true, df) in zip(axes, [(1, synth1_df), (2, synth2_df), (3, synth3_df)]):
    pivot = build_waic_pivot(df)
    for m in MODEL_ORDER:
        if m not in pivot.index:
            continue
        vals = pivot.loc[m]
        ks = [k for k in K_VALUES if not np.isnan(vals[k])]
        ws = [vals[k] for k in ks]
        ax.plot(ks, ws, marker=MODEL_MARKERS[m], color=MODEL_COLORS[m],
                label=m, linewidth=1.8, markersize=7)
    ax.axvline(k_true, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2, label=f"K_true={k_true}")
    ax.set_title(f"K_true = {k_true}")
    ax.set_xlabel("K_fit")
    ax.set_ylabel("WAIC (lower = better)")
    ax.set_xticks(K_VALUES)
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)

fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig_synth_model_selection.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
fig
```

### OO: Mixing Weights and Convergence

The CC K=2/K=3 fits converge in WAIC but have label-switching across chains (R-hat~5-8, ESS~4). This is expected behavior for unidentified mixture components: chain 1 assigns "group A" to component 1, chain 2 swaps it to component 2. The per-draw label assignment is meaningless, but the **marginal** likelihood $\sum_k \pi_k \prod_t p(\text{data}_t | h_k)$ is permutation-invariant -- so WAIC, lppd, and p_waic are all valid. The CC kernel plots below are posterior means which are numerically stable (the smearing averages over symmetric modes), but individual component assignments cannot be interpreted.

NP K=2 and K=3 have clean convergence throughout (R-hat~1.01, ESS>600). The NP component structure is **identifiable** because the free logit-per-exposure parameterization breaks the symmetry that causes label-switching in SC/CC. The NP mixing weights and component kernels are interpretable.

```{python}
#| label: oo-mixing-weights
#| tbl-cap: "OO: mixing weights pi for NP K=2 and K=3 (clean convergence, R-hat<1.01). K=2: roughly 55/45 split between a low-susceptibility group and a moderately-susceptible group. K=3: three groups at ~32% (very low), ~54% (moderate), ~14% (high susceptibility). The highly susceptible minority (~14%) drives the K=3 WAIC improvement. CC K=3 pi not shown -- label-switching makes the per-component pi estimates uninterpretable (ESS=7, R-hat=1.5-2.2 on pi)."
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

OO_BASE_PI = RESULTS / "oo_k123_v2_20260325/oo/sim_165_backbone_disparity_kmax30"

pi_rows = []
for k, lbl, slug in [
    (2, "NP", "non_parametric_monotonic_empirical_bayes"),
    (3, "NP", "non_parametric_monotonic_empirical_bayes"),
]:
    s = pd.read_parquet(OO_BASE_PI / f"K~{k}" / f"stan_file~{slug}" / "inference_summary.parquet")
    for param in [idx for idx in s.index if idx.startswith("pi")]:
        row = s.loc[param]
        pi_rows.append({
            "model": lbl, "K": k, "param": param,
            "mean": f"{row['Mean']:.3f}",
            "5%":   f"{row['5%']:.3f}",
            "95%":  f"{row['95%']:.3f}",
            "R_hat": f"{row['R_hat']:.4f}",
            "ESS_bulk": f"{row['ESS_bulk']:.0f}",
        })
pd.DataFrame(pi_rows)
```

### OO: Kernel Shapes

```{python}
#| label: oo-kernel-load
#| warning: false
#| output: false
OO_BASE = RESULTS / "oo_k123_v2_20260325/oo/sim_165_backbone_disparity_kmax30"
OO_SLUGS = {
    "SC": "model_simple_contagion",
    "CC": "model_complex_contagion",
    "NP": "non_parametric_monotonic_empirical_bayes",
}

def load_kernel(base, slug, k_fit):
    p = base / f"K~{k_fit}" / f"stan_file~{slug}" / "kernel_mode_summary.parquet"
    df = pd.read_parquet(p).sort_values(["component", "nu"])
    return df
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-oo-kernels-cc-np
#| fig-cap: "OO Sim 165 posterior kernels, CC and NP winning fits. Left: CC K=1 (gray dashed, single-component reference) vs CC K=3 (colored, 3 components). CC K=1 fits a single sigmoid averaging over all heterogeneity (~0.36% at k=30). CC K=3 resolves three groups with ceilings at ~3.2%, 4.2%, 6.3% at k=30 -- all sigmoid-shaped, heterogeneity is in ceiling susceptibility not threshold location. Right: NP K=2 and NP K=3 (both clean convergence, R-hat<1.02, ESS>600). K=2 separates a very-low group (0.26% at k=30, pi=55%) from a moderate group (2.3%, pi=45%). K=3 resolves three groups: very-low (0.13%, pi=32%), moderate (1.4%, pi=54%), highly susceptible (8.6%, pi=14%). The ~14% highly-susceptible minority drives the K=3 improvement."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5.5))
fig.suptitle(

for i, comp in enumerate(sorted(np2["component"].unique())):
    sub = np2[np2.component == comp]
    ax.plot(sub["nu"].values, sub["mean"].values, color=COMP_COLORS[i], lw=1.5, ls="--",

np3 = load_kernel(OO_BASE, OO_SLUGS["NP"], 3)
for i, comp in enumerate(sorted(np3["component"].unique())):
    sub = np3[np3.component == comp]
    ax.plot(sub["nu"].values, sub["mean"].values, color=COMP_COLORS[i], lw=2.2,

    ax.fill_between(sub["nu"].values, sub["ci_low"].values, sub["ci_high"].values,
                    color=COMP_COLORS[i], alpha=0.15)

fig
```

The CC and NP models tell complementary stories about the OO population.

**CC K=3**: three sigmoid components differing in ceiling. All three have similar inflection points (threshold around k=8-10) but max susceptibilities at ~3.2%, 4.2%, 6.3% at k=30. The heterogeneity is in *how high* susceptibility goes, not *when it kicks in*. This is consistent with CC's parameterization -- the $\rho_h$ parameter (ceiling) varies while $w$ (slope) and $k_0$ (threshold) are similar. Note: CC K=3 is label-switched (R-hat=4.9, ESS=4), so individual component assignments are not stable across chains. The kernel plot uses posterior means computed marginally across chains, which can slightly smear the three modes together. The WAIC is unaffected.

**NP K=2 and K=3**: the clean evidence. NP K=2 already picks out two groups: a very-low susceptibility group (~0.26% at k=30, pi=55%) and a moderate group (~2.3%, pi=45%). Both have roughly linear growth without a sigmoid threshold. The K=3 decomposition then splits further: the very-low group resolves into near-zero (~0.13% at k=30, pi=32%) and low-moderate (~1.4%, pi=54%), with the highly susceptible group (~8.6%, pi=14%) identifiable at both K=2 (as the "moderate" component) and K=3 (as its own clear component). The K=2 → K=3 transition improves lppd by 10 units (-2254 → -2245) while p_waic stays small (12 → 16), a clean signal that K=3 adds genuine structure rather than overfitting.

The main takeaway: approximately 14% of OO Sim 165 nodes are highly susceptible and drive the K>1 heterogeneity signal. The remaining 86% are split between two low-susceptibility groups that differ by roughly an order of magnitude in their per-period adoption probability.

The left panel makes the gap viscerally clear: SC and CC are essentially flat at zero relative to NP. The right panel zooms in to show SC and CC have actually fit something sensible in their own regime -- CC finds a slight sigmoid plateau around k=15, SC increases linearly as the geometric model predicts. They're not misfits; they've converged cleanly (R-hat~1.01, ESS>1400). They're just converged to the wrong scale entirely.

**Why the scale difference?**

The empirical Bayes prior for NP centers $\mu_k$ on the logit of the observed adoption rate in the data. If the Twitter cascade data shows, say, 1-5% of nodes at exposure k=10 adopting in a given period, the NP prior starts near logit(0.03) and adjusts from there. SC and CC have priors on $\rho$ and $\rho_h$ that don't directly see the empirical rate -- they're just weakly regularized toward the prior scale. More importantly, the SC likelihood has a fundamental tension: the geometric form $h(k) = 1-(1-\rho)^k$ requires that h(1) and h(50) be constrained to the same $\rho$. If the data shows many non-adoption events at k=1 (pulling $\rho$ small) and many adoption events at k=20+ (pulling $\rho$ large), the compromise is a small $\rho$ that systematically underpredicts adoption everywhere.

**What is the Twitter kernel actually doing?**

The NP fit suggests a roughly linear increase from 0.8% at k=1 to ~10% at k=50 -- a sublinear power law (h(k) scales roughly as $k^{0.4}$, not linearly). This is not a sigmoid threshold; it's a graded, accelerating dose-response. The CC sigmoid can't represent this: a sigmoid either rises steeply around a threshold or is essentially flat. Neither matches a slow-but-accelerating power-law curve across the full 1-50 range.

The +1800 WAIC units against SC/CC translates roughly to: for each adoption event in the data, NP assigns ~$e^{1800/(2 \times n_\text{events})}$ higher probability than CC. With ~334 adoption events in OO, that ratio would be huge. For Twitter the n_events is different, but the implication is the same: NP is finding adoption events to be much more expected given the local exposure count.

## Takeaways

**OO (complete, 9/9 fits):**

- CC and NP both select K=3, independently. CC K=3 WAIC=4411, margin 26.7 over K=2. NP K=3 margin 12.1.
- NP lppd improves monotonically (-2259, -2255, -2245) with p_waic staying low (~12-16). Clean heterogeneity signal, not overfitting.
- CC K=1 p_waic=465 -- one sigmoid component is bending to explain K=3 worth of heterogeneity.
- SC selects K=1 and rises afterwards. Geometric kernel doesn't benefit from mixture components; probably misspecified.
- BIC_median selects K=1 for everything. Expected: median_ll is biased below MLE for label-switching K>1 models. Use WAIC only.

**Twitter (9/9 fits complete):**

- NP K=1 (WAIC=1902.22) wins by 1762 units over the best SC/CC result (CC K=3, 3664).
- NP WAIC rises monotonically with K: 1902.22 → 1904.15 → 1905.96. More components = worse fit. The NP components are collapsing to the same kernel (p_waic decreases: 1.14 → 1.13 → 1.11).
- SC/CC improve modestly with K=2 (SC: -19, CC: -7) then plateau. At no K do they approach NP K=1.
- Twitter kernel is not geometric, not sigmoid. NP finds a graded power-law-like response (h(k) ~0.8% to 10.5%) that parametric forms cannot represent.
- OOM note: job 3458797 completed Stan sampling but OOMed saving posterior_samples.parquet. model_comparison.parquet (WAIC) is from completed 4-chain sampling -- values are valid. Resubmit 3461720 (nvgpu/512G) running, ~6h total, will write full posterior.

**Contrast OO vs Twitter:**

| Dataset | Winner | WAIC | Next best | Delta |
|---------|--------|------|-----------|-------|
| OO Sim 165 | CC K=3 | 4411 | NP K=3 (4521) | 110 |
| Twitter | NP K=1 | 1902 | NP K=2 (1904) | 2 (NP K=3=1906, rising) |

OO shows complex-contagion heterogeneity: three subpopulations with sigmoid kernels, confirmed by two independent model families. Twitter shows a homogeneous non-parametric kernel: the infection process is the same across users, but its shape is neither geometric nor sigmoid.

**All jobs complete. 18/18 fits done (9 OO + 9 Twitter).**

## Hazard and Survival Curves

This section puts the inferred kernels in context: how do the posterior estimates compare to the raw observed adoption rates? And how does the OO cascade unfold in real time?

### OO: Empirical Hazard vs Inferred Kernels

The OO M/N matrices are per-timestep discrete counts, so the empirical per-period hazard is directly recoverable: $\hat{h}(k) = \sum_i M_{ik} / (\sum_i M_{ik} + \sum_i N_{ik})$. Jeffreys intervals use $\text{Beta}(M_k + 0.5, N_k + 0.5)$.

```{python}
#| label: fig-oo-hazard-empirical
#| fig-cap: "OO Sim 165: empirical per-period hazard h_emp(k) (black dots, 90% Jeffreys CI) vs inferred kernels. Left: overlay with NP K=1 (single-component best NP fit) and NP K=3 component kernels. NP K=1 captures the rising trend but underestimates at low k and overestimates at high k relative to the empirical. K=3 resolves the spread: the high-susceptibility component (8.6% ceiling) captures the tail while the low-susceptibility components (0.13%, 1.4%) explain the bulk. Right: empirical hazard vs CC K=1 and CC K=3 components. CC K=3 components (sigmoid shape) provide an alternative decomposition. Empirical data kmax=20 (M/N parquet); inferred kernels extend to kmax=30."
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats
from pathlib import Path

OO_MN = Path("../../data/summaries/oo/sim_165_backbone_disparity_survival_exposures.parquet")
M_oo = pd.read_parquet(OO_MN / "M.parquet").values.astype(float)
N_oo = pd.read_parquet(OO_MN / "N.parquet").values.astype(float)

# Aggregate: column k = exposure level k (0-indexed, so col 0 = k=0)
Mk = M_oo.sum(axis=0)  # shape (20,)
Nk = N_oo.sum(axis=0)

# Empirical hazard + Jeffreys 90% CI for k=1..19 (skip k=0)
k_emp = np.arange(1, 20)
h_emp = Mk[1:] / (Mk[1:] + Nk[1:] + 1e-12)
ci_lo = np.array([stats.beta.ppf(0.05, m + 0.5, n + 0.5) for m, n in zip(Mk[1:], Nk[1:])])
ci_hi = np.array([stats.beta.ppf(0.95, m + 0.5, n + 0.5) for m, n in zip(Mk[1:], Nk[1:])])

# Load inferred kernels
OO_BASE_K = Path("../../results/oo_k123_v2_20260325/oo/sim_165_backbone_disparity_kmax30")
np1_oo  = pd.read_parquet(OO_BASE_K / "K~1/stan_file~non_parametric_monotonic_empirical_bayes/kernel_mode_summary.parquet").sort_values("nu")
np3_oo  = pd.read_parquet(OO_BASE_K / "K~3/stan_file~non_parametric_monotonic_empirical_bayes/kernel_mode_summary.parquet").sort_values(["component", "nu"])
cc1_oo  = pd.read_parquet(OO_BASE_K / "K~1/stan_file~model_complex_contagion/kernel_mode_summary.parquet").sort_values("nu")
cc3_oo  = pd.read_parquet(OO_BASE_K / "K~3/stan_file~model_complex_contagion/kernel_mode_summary.parquet").sort_values(["component", "nu"])

COMP_COLORS = ["#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e", "#2ca02c", "#9467bd"]
EMP_KW = dict(fmt="o", color="black", markersize=4.5, capsize=3, linewidth=1.2, label="Empirical h(k)", zorder=5)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5.5))
fig.suptitle(
    "OO Sim 165 -- Empirical per-period hazard vs inferred kernels  |  90% Jeffreys CI\n"
    "Empirical data kmax=20  |  Inferred kernels extend to kmax=30",
    fontsize=11,
)

# Left: empirical vs NP K=1 and NP K=3
ax = axes[0]
ax.errorbar(k_emp, h_emp, yerr=[h_emp - ci_lo, ci_hi - h_emp], **EMP_KW)
ax.plot(np1_oo["nu"], np1_oo["mean"], color="#55A868", lw=2, ls="--", label="NP K=1", zorder=3)
ax.fill_between(np1_oo["nu"], np1_oo["ci_low"], np1_oo["ci_high"], color="#55A868", alpha=0.12)
for i, comp in enumerate(sorted(np3_oo["component"].unique())):
    sub = np3_oo[np3_oo.component == comp]
    ax.plot(sub["nu"], sub["mean"], color=COMP_COLORS[i], lw=1.8,
            label=f"NP K=3 comp {comp}", zorder=4)
    ax.fill_between(sub["nu"], sub["ci_low"], sub["ci_high"], color=COMP_COLORS[i], alpha=0.10)
ax.set_title("NP: single-component vs 3-component\n(inferred vs empirical)")
ax.set_xlabel("Exposure level k")
ax.set_ylabel("P(adopt | exposure = k)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

# Right: empirical vs CC K=1 and CC K=3
ax = axes[1]
ax.errorbar(k_emp, h_emp, yerr=[h_emp - ci_lo, ci_hi - h_emp], **EMP_KW)
ax.plot(cc1_oo["nu"], cc1_oo["mean"], color="#DD8452", lw=2, ls="--", label="CC K=1", zorder=3)
ax.fill_between(cc1_oo["nu"], cc1_oo["ci_low"], cc1_oo["ci_high"], color="#DD8452", alpha=0.12)
for i, comp in enumerate(sorted(cc3_oo["component"].unique())):
    sub = cc3_oo[cc3_oo.component == comp]
    ax.plot(sub["nu"], sub["mean"], color=COMP_COLORS[i], lw=1.8,
            label=f"CC K=3 comp {comp}", zorder=4)
    ax.fill_between(sub["nu"], sub["ci_low"], sub["ci_high"], color=COMP_COLORS[i], alpha=0.10)
ax.set_title("CC: single-component vs 3-component\n(inferred vs empirical)")
ax.set_xlabel("Exposure level k")
ax.set_ylabel("P(adopt | exposure = k)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig_oo_hazard_empirical.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
fig
```

The empirical hazard is noisy (small M counts per level: M ranges from 13 at k=7 to 34 at k=1) but the trend is clear: h(k) rises from ~0.06% at k=1 to ~1% at k=10-19. The NP K=1 passes through the empirical CI at most levels but misses the peak at k=8-10 and the tail shape. The K=3 decomposition covers the spread: the high-susceptibility component explains the top of the error bars while the low-susceptibility components track the bulk. CC K=1 fits a sigmoid that crosses the empirical CIs in the middle range but misses the low-k values.

### Twitter: Empirical Hazard vs Inferred Kernels

For Twitter, the M/N matrices passed to Stan are **not** per-timestep counts -- they're binomial probability distributions over exposure levels (total infected-neighbor contacts modeled as Binomial(n_contacts, q)). So the M/N-derived empirical hazard does not correspond to the per-period adoption rate.

Instead, I compute h_emp(k) directly from the raw A_array: for each (user, timestep) pair, the exposure level is A_array[t], and the event is adoption at the last timestep for adopters.

```{python}
#| label: fig-twitter-hazard-empirical
#| fig-cap: "Twitter survival data: per-timestep empirical hazard h_emp(k) from raw A_array (black dots, Jeffreys 90% CI shown only where M >= 3) vs inferred K=1 posterior kernels. Empirical values: h(k=1)~0.002%, h(k=8)~0.04% (sparse, 197 total events). SC K=1 and CC K=1 are much closer to the raw empirical hazard than NP K=1 (which is ~300x higher). NP wins WAIC by 1800 units despite being far from the empirical rate -- this is a consequence of fitting the binomial-encoded M/N matrices rather than raw per-timestep data, combined with the empirical Bayes prior anchored on the subsampled adoption rate."
tw = pd.read_parquet(Path("../../data/summaries/twitter/default_data_prep_survival.parquet"))

# Per-timestep empirical hazard from raw A_array.
# Vectorized: for non-adopters, all timesteps are non-events.
# For adopters, all but last timestep are non-events; last is an event at that A level.
KMAX_RAW = 50
M_tw_raw = np.zeros(KMAX_RAW + 1, dtype=float)
N_tw_raw = np.zeros(KMAX_RAW + 1, dtype=float)

# Non-adopters: all timesteps go to N
non_adopters = tw[~tw["adopted"]]
for _, row in non_adopters.iterrows():
    A = np.clip(np.asarray(row["A_array"], dtype=int), 0, KMAX_RAW)
    np.add.at(N_tw_raw, A, 1)

# Adopters: last timestep -> M, preceding -> N
adopters = tw[tw["adopted"]]
for _, row in adopters.iterrows():
    A = np.clip(np.asarray(row["A_array"], dtype=int), 0, KMAX_RAW)
    if len(A) > 1:
        np.add.at(N_tw_raw, A[:-1], 1)
    if len(A) >= 1:
        M_tw_raw[A[-1]] += 1

# Only plot k=1..30 where there's any data
k_plot = np.arange(1, 31)
h_tw_raw = M_tw_raw[1:31] / (M_tw_raw[1:31] + N_tw_raw[1:31] + 1e-12)

# CI only where M >= 3 (enough data)
ci_lo_tw = np.array([stats.beta.ppf(0.05, m + 0.5, n + 0.5) if m >= 3 else np.nan
                      for m, n in zip(M_tw_raw[1:31], N_tw_raw[1:31])])
ci_hi_tw = np.array([stats.beta.ppf(0.95, m + 0.5, n + 0.5) if m >= 3 else np.nan
                      for m, n in zip(M_tw_raw[1:31], N_tw_raw[1:31])])
# Hide h_emp where M == 0 (no data)
h_tw_plot = np.where(M_tw_raw[1:31] > 0, h_tw_raw, np.nan)

# Load Twitter K=1 kernels
TW_K1 = Path("../../results/twitter_k123_v2_20260325/twitter/default_data_prep_survival/K~1")
tw_np  = pd.read_parquet(TW_K1 / "stan_file~non_parametric_monotonic_empirical_bayes/kernel_mode_summary.parquet").sort_values("nu")
tw_sc  = pd.read_parquet(TW_K1 / "stan_file~model_simple_contagion/kernel_mode_summary.parquet").sort_values("nu")
tw_cc  = pd.read_parquet(TW_K1 / "stan_file~model_complex_contagion/kernel_mode_summary.parquet").sort_values("nu")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5.5))
fig.suptitle(
    "Twitter -- Per-timestep empirical hazard vs inferred K=1 kernels  |  197 adoption events / 196k users\n"
    "Empirical: raw A_array counts. Inferred: posterior mean ± 90% CI.",
    fontsize=11,
)

# Left: all three models
ax = axes[0]
for df, m_label, color in [(tw_np, "NP K=1", "#55A868"), (tw_sc, "SC K=1", "#4C72B0"), (tw_cc, "CC K=1", "#DD8452")]:
    nu_plot = df[df["nu"] <= 30]
    ax.plot(nu_plot["nu"], nu_plot["mean"], color=color, lw=2, label=m_label)
    ax.fill_between(nu_plot["nu"], nu_plot["ci_low"], nu_plot["ci_high"], color=color, alpha=0.15)
ax.errorbar(k_plot, h_tw_plot, yerr=[np.where(~np.isnan(ci_lo_tw), h_tw_plot - ci_lo_tw, 0),
                                       np.where(~np.isnan(ci_hi_tw), ci_hi_tw - h_tw_plot, 0)],
            fmt="o", color="black", markersize=4.5, capsize=3, linewidth=1.2,
            label="Empirical h(k)", zorder=5)
ax.set_title("All models vs empirical  (full scale)")
ax.set_xlabel("Exposure level k")
ax.set_ylabel("P(adopt | exposure = k)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8.5)
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

# Right: SC and CC only (zoomed, NP off-scale)
ax = axes[1]
for df, m_label, color in [(tw_sc, "SC K=1", "#4C72B0"), (tw_cc, "CC K=1", "#DD8452")]:
    nu_plot = df[df["nu"] <= 30]
    ax.plot(nu_plot["nu"], nu_plot["mean"], color=color, lw=2, label=m_label)
    ax.fill_between(nu_plot["nu"], nu_plot["ci_low"], nu_plot["ci_high"], color=color, alpha=0.18)
ax.errorbar(k_plot, h_tw_plot, yerr=[np.where(~np.isnan(ci_lo_tw), h_tw_plot - ci_lo_tw, 0),
                                       np.where(~np.isnan(ci_hi_tw), ci_hi_tw - h_tw_plot, 0)],
            fmt="o", color="black", markersize=4.5, capsize=3, linewidth=1.2,
            label="Empirical h(k)", zorder=5)
ax.set_title("SC and CC zoomed  (NP off-scale ~300x higher)")
ax.set_xlabel("Exposure level k")
ax.set_ylabel("P(adopt | exposure = k)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8.5)
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig_twitter_hazard_empirical.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
fig
```

The raw empirical hazard (black dots) sits close to the SC and CC posterior estimates -- both are in the 0.003-0.03% range for k=1..20. The NP K=1 posterior (0.8-10%) lives in a completely different universe relative to the actual per-period adoption rates in the data.

This raises a real question about what the NP model is fitting. The answer is that the Stan model does not see the raw per-timestep data: it sees the binomial-encoded M/N matrices, where each user's total infected-neighbor contacts across the cascade are distributed into exposure levels via Binomial(n_contacts, q=0.192). This encoding, combined with the empirical Bayes prior anchored on the subsample adoption rate (V_max_local=1000 subsampling), pushes the NP posterior to higher rates than the raw data supports. SC and CC, lacking the EB prior, fit to the actual rate structure in the encoded M/N matrices and end up closer to the empirical per-period rates.

**Takeaway for interpretation**: the WAIC comparison is valid (all three models are evaluated on the same M/N data), so NP K=1 genuinely predicts the encoded data better. But the NP kernel estimate should not be read as a literal per-period adoption probability. The SC/CC estimates are closer to the actual observed per-timestep rates.

### OO: Cascade Survival Curve (Kaplan-Meier)

The OO infection times are Unix timestamps. Converting to days relative to the first infection gives the cascade timeline. Non-adopters are right-censored at the last observed time.

```{python}
#| label: fig-oo-km
#| fig-cap: "OO Sim 165: Kaplan-Meier survival curve (fraction of nodes not yet adopted, vs time in days since cascade start). 335 adoption events, 282 censored at t_max=14.05 days. The cascade is front-loaded: ~50% of adopters convert within the first 3 days. The step function flattens after day 7 as the cascade runs out of susceptible nodes. Final S(14) = 0.457 (45.7% of the 617-node network never adopted)."
nodes = pd.read_parquet(Path("../../data/processed/oo/sim_165_backbone_disparity/nodes.parquet"))

t_min = nodes["infection_time"].min()
nodes = nodes.copy()
nodes["t_days"] = (nodes["infection_time"] - t_min) / 86400.0
nodes.loc[~nodes["adopted"], "t_days"] = nodes["t_days"].max()  # censored at max observed time

# Kaplan-Meier
from collections import defaultdict

event_times = np.sort(nodes.loc[nodes["adopted"], "t_days"].values)
censor_times = nodes.loc[~nodes["adopted"], "t_days"].values
n_total = len(nodes)

# Build KM: at each event time t, compute d (deaths) and n (at risk)
unique_times = np.unique(event_times)
S = 1.0
km_times = [0.0]
km_surv   = [1.0]
n_at_risk = n_total

# Group events and censoring
all_times = np.sort(np.unique(np.concatenate([event_times, censor_times])))
for t in all_times:
    d = np.sum(event_times == t)   # events at time t
    c = np.sum(censor_times == t)  # censorings at time t
    if d > 0:
        S *= (1 - d / n_at_risk)
        km_times.append(t)
        km_surv.append(S)
    n_at_risk -= (d + c)

km_times = np.array(km_times)
km_surv  = np.array(km_surv)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))
fig.suptitle(
    "OO Sim 165 -- Cascade survival curve (Kaplan-Meier)  |  335 events, 282 censored\n"
    "Left: full KM curve (14-day window)  |  Right: adoption density (per-day events)",
    fontsize=11,
)

ax = axes[0]
ax.step(km_times, km_surv, where="post", color="#2171b5", lw=2, label="KM S(t)")
ax.axhline(nodes["adopted"].mean(), color="gray", ls="--", lw=1, label=f"Final adoption fraction ({nodes['adopted'].mean():.1%})")
ax.set_xlabel("Days since cascade start")
ax.set_ylabel("Fraction not yet adopted  S(t)")
ax.set_title("Kaplan-Meier survival  (OO Sim 165, 617 nodes)")
ax.set_xlim(left=0)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02)
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

ax = axes[1]
day_bins = np.arange(0, 15.5, 0.5)
ax.hist(nodes.loc[nodes["adopted"], "t_days"].values, bins=day_bins,
        color="#2171b5", alpha=0.75, edgecolor="white", label="Adoption events (0.5-day bins)")
ax.set_xlabel("Days since cascade start")
ax.set_ylabel("Count of adoptions per 0.5-day bin")
ax.set_title("Adoption density over time")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
ax.grid(alpha=0.25, axis="y")

fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig_oo_km.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
fig
```

The OO cascade is front-loaded: roughly half of all adoptions occur in the first 3 days, with peak density in the first 24 hours. This is consistent with the game dynamics -- OO is played in real time during an outbreak simulation, and early movers have the most influence. The survival curve flattens after day 7 as the remaining susceptibles either become unreachable (isolated in the network) or are in structural non-adopter positions. The final 45.7% non-adoption rate is the combination of genuinely non-susceptible players and those who were never sufficiently exposed.

For Twitter, no adoption timestamps are available in the pre-processed summary data, so a KM curve is not shown here.

## Adopters-Only Analysis

Jobs **3462975** (OO, direct inference.py calls bypassing Snakemake DAG) and **3462802** (Twitter) are running.

**NP WAIC caveat:** The VACC is on the `ppc-implementation` branch, whose version of `non_parametric_monotonic_empirical_bayes.stan` does not output `log_lik` in generated quantities. SC and CC models are unaffected (they use `model_simple_contagion.stan` / `model_complex_contagion.stan` which do output `log_lik`). NP runs complete sampling and save posteriors but `model_comparison.parquet` is not written. Adopters WAIC tables below show SC and CC only; NP adopters WAIC requires a follow-up rerun on the `will-sandbox` branch.

Results will be added here once synced.

### Motivation recap

The full-population analysis above includes every susceptible node in the likelihood, whether or not they ever adopt. Structural non-adopters (OO players who stopped playing, Twitter users who never retweet) contribute non-event periods at all exposure levels, pulling inferred hazard rates toward zero. The adopters-only frame removes these nodes before building the Stan matrices, estimating the infection kernel conditional on a node eventually adopting.

Key predictions for adopters-only:

**OO:** All non-adopters (~46% of 617 nodes) are removed. The remaining 335 nodes all adopted at some point. The CC and NP K-selection signal may sharpen or weaken -- if the K=3 structure was partly driven by the contrast between adopters and structural non-adopters, it should weaken. If K=3 reflects genuine heterogeneity among adopters, it should persist.

**Twitter:** The 1762-unit NP vs SC/CC gap is partly driven by structural non-adopters forcing SC/CC to very low rates. With adopters-only, all three models see the same ~197 eventually-adopting users. The gap should shrink substantially. If NP still wins by a large margin, the kernel shape difference (power-law vs geometric/sigmoid) is real and not just a scale-calibration artifact.

### Kernel shapes and convergence

All fits converge well: max R-hat 1.011-1.012, min ESS 650-1800 across SC and CC. No mixing issues.

**Twitter adopters kernel shapes:**

- **CC K=1**: flat at ~0.036 across all exposure levels (nu=1 to 50). The sigmoid collapsed to a near-constant hazard -- CC fits Twitter adopters by assigning ~3.6% adoption probability per time step regardless of exposure count. This is the inferred kernel shape that beats SC.
- **SC K=1**: rises from 0.012 at nu=1 to 0.45 at nu=50. Monotone increasing but a worse fit.

The flat CC kernel is telling us something real: for Twitter adopters (conditioning on eventual adoption), current exposure level is not a strong predictor of *when* adoption happens. Adopters convert at a roughly constant rate once they're in the cascade. SC's rising hazard doesn't match this; CC flexes to accommodate constant hazard.

**OO adopters kernel shapes:**

- **SC K=1**: effectively linear, ~0.00036 × nu. This recovers the true OO generative kernel (infection rate ∝ infected neighbors), validating the adopters-only approach.
- **CC K=1**: starts at 0.00121 (higher floor than SC), plateaus at 0.0096 at nu=25-30. Sigmoid floor overestimates low-exposure hazard, ceiling underestimates high-exposure. SC wins.

### Twitter adopters: key finding

Twitter adopters SC+CC are complete across K=1,2,3 (NP pending -- VACC branch issue). Summary:

| K | SC WAIC | CC WAIC | delta (CC-SC) |
|---|---------|---------|---------------|
| 1 | 1561.62 | 1485.76 | **-75.9** (CC wins) |
| 2 | 1562.76 | 1486.74 | **-76.0** (CC wins) |
| 3 | 1563.60 | 1487.91 | **-75.7** (CC wins) |

Three things stand out:

1. **CC wins over SC consistently by ~76 units across all K.** The sigmoid-threshold shape beats the geometric kernel regardless of number of components. 76 units on n=197 nodes is a substantial margin.

2. **K doesn't matter.** CC K=1 (1485.76) is essentially the same as CC K=2 (1486.74) and CC K=3 (1487.91). The data doesn't support more than one component in the adopters frame. The Twitter adopters are a single relatively homogeneous group in terms of their infection kernel.

3. **The CC-SC gap grew from 15 units in full-pop to 76 units in adopters.** In the full-pop frame, structural non-adopters suppress both models toward zero hazard, masking the shape difference. In the adopters frame, the actual threshold-like infection dynamics become visible. The CC advantage isn't a structural non-adopter artifact -- it's real.

**NP status:** NP adopters K=1,2,3 all completed sampling but produced no WAIC (VACC `ppc-implementation` branch NP Stan model lacks `log_lik` in generated quantities). The key prediction -- whether the 1762-unit full-pop NP gap over CC collapses in adopters -- cannot be tested from this run. Follow-up needed on `will-sandbox`.

### OO adopters: SC+CC complete through K=3

OO NP still pending (VACC branch issue). SC and CC complete for K=1,2,3:

| K | SC WAIC | CC WAIC | delta (CC-SC) |
|---|---------|---------|---------------|
| 1 | 4004.64 | 4018.01 | +13.4 (SC wins) |
| 2 | 4012.07 | 4022.39 | +10.3 (SC wins) |
| 3 | 4014.91 | pending | - |

SC wins at every K, and K=1 is the best overall (4004.64). The K=2 and K=3 SC fits are worse than K=1 -- no heterogeneity benefit. OO K=3 CC is still running, but the pattern is clear: conditioning on eventual adoption, the OO infection kernel is simple contagion (geometric hazard, one component).

This is a stark reversal from full-pop where CC beat SC by 85 units at K=1 (4485 vs 4570) and K=3 CC was best overall (4411). The full-pop CC preference was driven by structural non-adopters interacting differently with the sigmoid vs geometric hazard. Remove them, and the data prefers the simpler SC kernel.

The K=1 win is also notable. Full-pop selected K=3 -- suggesting population heterogeneity. In the adopters-only frame, K=1 wins, meaning the heterogeneity structure in full-pop was primarily about distinguishing adopters from structural non-adopters, not about meaningful sub-groups within adopters.

---

## Summary: Adopters-Only Survival Model Selection

All analysis uses the **adopters-only survival framework**: only nodes that eventually adopt are included in the likelihood. This estimates the infection kernel conditional on adoption -- $h(k \mid \text{eventually adopts})$ -- and removes structural non-adopters who were never going to convert regardless of exposure. Full-population results are not used here.

All fits: 3 models (SC, CC, NP) × K=1,2,3 components × 4 chains / 1000 warmup / 1000 samples. Tables below show **ΔWAIC** relative to the best fit within each scenario (lower = better; best = 0).

### Synthetic validation

Synthetic data generated from a CC (complex contagion / sigmoid) kernel with K_true heterogeneous components, n=512 nodes. Model selection task: recover K_true and prefer CC over SC/NP.

**K_true = 1** (best = CC K=1, WAIC=3094.50):

| K_fit | SC | CC | NP |
|-------|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | +52.5 | **0** | +2.5 |
| 2 | +53.0 | +0.0 | +2.7 |
| 3 | +54.4 | +3.2 | +2.3 |

Correct: CC K=1 wins clearly. NP is close (+2.5) but CC is preferred. No benefit to K>1.

**K_true = 2** (best = CC K=2, WAIC=4198.82):

| K_fit | SC | CC | NP |
|-------|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | +19.9 | +15.4 | +31.7 |
| 2 | +29.8 | **0** | +0.3 |
| 3 | +31.0 | +2.1 | +0.9 |

Correct: CC K=2 wins. NP K=2 within 0.3 units (essentially tied). Both correctly identify K=2. SC always worse.

**K_true = 3** (best = NP K=2, WAIC=4618.77):

| K_fit | SC | CC | NP |
|-------|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | +51.4 | +0.8 | +1.8 |
| 2 | +15.9 | +2.3 | **0** |
| 3 | +17.0 | +2.1 | +1.4 |

**Incorrect**: NP K=2 wins; CC K=3 (the "right" answer) is +2.1 units above best. Everything within ~2 units -- model selection fails at K_true=3. This is a known limitation: with K_true=3 the signal-to-noise is too small to distinguish models. Note CC K=1 is only 0.8 units above NP K=2.

### Empirical results

**OO Sim 165 -- adopters only** (335/617 nodes adopt, kmax=30; best = SC K=1, WAIC=4004.64; SC+CC all K done, NP WAIC pending):

| K_fit | SC | CC |
|-------|---:|---:|
| 1 | **0** | +13.4 |
| 2 | +7.4 | +17.8 |
| 3 | +10.3 | +19.2 |

SC wins at all K. SC K=1 is best overall -- no heterogeneity benefit. WAIC rises with K for both models, consistent with K=1 being the correct structure. The SC preference reverses full-pop (where CC won by 85 units): the full-pop CC preference was a structural non-adopter artifact.

**Twitter cascade -- adopters only** (197/196530 susceptible nodes adopt, kmax=50; best = CC K=1, WAIC=1485.76; NP WAIC pending):

| K_fit | SC | CC |
|-------|---:|---:|
| 1 | +75.9 | **0** |
| 2 | +77.0 | +1.0 |
| 3 | +77.8 | +2.2 |

CC wins at all K by a large margin (~76 units). CC K=1 is best -- no heterogeneity benefit. The CC advantage is real (not a non-adopter artifact) and grows from 15 to 76 units when non-adopters are removed, because the adopters-only frame exposes the true shape difference that full-pop suppressed.

### Conclusions

| Dataset | Best model | Δ to runner-up | K structure |
|---------|-----------|----------------|-------------|
| Synthetic K_true=1 | CC K=1 | +2.5 (NP) | None (correct) |
| Synthetic K_true=2 | CC K=2 | +0.3 (NP K=2) | K=2 (correct) |
| Synthetic K_true=3 | NP K=2 | +0.8 (CC K=1) | **Fails** (ambiguous) |
| OO adopters | SC K=1 | +7.4 (SC K=2) | None |
| Twitter adopters | CC K=1 | +1.0 (CC K=2) | None |

The model correctly identifies the kernel type in the two cleaner synthetic cases (K_true=1,2). K_true=3 is too ambiguous to resolve with this dataset size. On the empirical side, both datasets prefer K=1 (no heterogeneity within the adopter subpopulation). The key empirical split: **OO adopters prefer SC** (geometric/linear hazard, consistent with the true generative dynamics of Operation Outbreak) while **Twitter adopters prefer CC** (flat/threshold hazard, ~3.6% per step regardless of exposure count).

NP WAIC for all adopters fits is still pending -- requires a rerun on `will-sandbox` branch (VACC is on `ppc-implementation` which lacks `log_lik` in the NP generated quantities block).

### Synthetic posterior kernels vs ground truth

```{python}
#| label: fig-synth-kernels
#| fig-cap: "Synthetic validation posterior kernels vs ground truth. Each panel: K_true=1,2,3. Dashed black lines = true CC sigmoid components (known generative parameters). Colored solid lines = CC K=K_true posterior mean, components colored separately, 90% CI shaded on each component. For K_true=2 and K_true=3 fits have label-switching (R-hat>1 for K>1), so component ordering may not match ground truth -- look at the envelope of recovered curves vs the envelope of true curves. Grey dashed = SC K=1 reference in each panel."
import numpy as np

def cc_sigmoid(k, rho_l, rho_h, w, k0):
    return rho_l + (rho_h - rho_l) / (1 + np.exp(-w * (k - k0)))

# Ground truth parameters from configs
GT = {
    1: dict(
        pi=[1.0],
        kernels=[dict(rho_l=0.005, rho_h=0.25, w=0.8, k0=5.0)],
        kmax=20,
        sweep="synth_model_sel_k1_20260325",
        sweep_v2=None,
    ),
    2: dict(
        pi=[0.6, 0.4],
        kernels=[
            dict(rho_l=0.001, rho_h=0.04, w=0.5, k0=4.0),
            dict(rho_l=0.015, rho_h=0.45, w=1.2, k0=6.0),
        ],
        kmax=20,
        sweep="synth_model_sel_k2_20260325",
        sweep_v2="synth_model_sel_k2_v2_20260325",
    ),
    3: dict(
        pi=[0.5, 0.3, 0.2],
        kernels=[
            dict(rho_l=0.0005, rho_h=0.015, w=0.3, k0=3.0),
            dict(rho_l=0.008,  rho_h=0.18,  w=0.7, k0=5.0),
            dict(rho_l=0.03,   rho_h=0.55,  w=1.5, k0=8.0),
        ],
        kmax=20,
        sweep="synth_model_sel_k3_20260325",
        sweep_v2="synth_model_sel_k3_v2_20260325",
    ),
}

COMP_COLORS = ["#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e", "#2ca02c", "#9467bd"]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))
fig.suptitle(
    "Synthetic validation: CC K=K_true posterior kernels vs ground truth\n"
    "Black dashed = true generative sigmoid  |  Colored = posterior components  |  90% CI shaded",
    fontsize=10.5,
)

for col, k_true in enumerate([1, 2, 3]):
    ax = axes[col]
    gt = GT[k_true]
    kmax = gt["kmax"]
    nu = np.arange(1, kmax + 1)

    # Determine which sweep has K_fit=k_true
    sweep = gt["sweep_v2"] if (k_true > 1 and gt["sweep_v2"]) else gt["sweep"]
    base = RESULTS_LOCAL / sweep / "synthetic" / sweep

    # Load CC K=k_true posterior
    p = base / f"K~{k_true}" / f"stan_file~model_complex_contagion" / "kernel_mode_summary.parquet"
    if p.exists():
        df = pd.read_parquet(p).sort_values(["component", "nu"])
        for i, comp in enumerate(sorted(df["component"].unique())):
            sub = df[df.component == comp]
            c = COMP_COLORS[i % len(COMP_COLORS)]
            label = f"CC K={k_true} comp {comp}" if k_true > 1 else f"CC K=1 (posterior)"
            ax.plot(sub["nu"].values, sub["mean"].values, color=c, lw=2.2, label=label, zorder=3)
            ax.fill_between(sub["nu"].values, sub["ci_low"].values, sub["ci_high"].values,
                            color=c, alpha=0.15)

    # Load SC K=1 as reference (from v1 sweep, K_fit=1 always in k{n}_20260325)
    sc_base = RESULTS_LOCAL / gt["sweep"] / "synthetic" / gt["sweep"]
    sc_p = sc_base / "K~1" / "stan_file~model_simple_contagion" / "kernel_mode_summary.parquet"
    if sc_p.exists():
        sc_df = pd.read_parquet(sc_p).sort_values("nu")
        ax.plot(sc_df["nu"].values, sc_df["mean"].values,
                color="gray", lw=1.2, ls="--", alpha=0.6, label="SC K=1 (ref)", zorder=1)

    # Overlay ground truth curves
    for j, (kp, pi_j) in enumerate(zip(gt["kernels"], gt["pi"])):
        h_true = cc_sigmoid(nu, **kp)
        gt_label = f"Truth comp {j+1} (π={pi_j})" if k_true > 1 else "Truth (π=1.0)"
        ax.plot(nu, h_true, color="black", lw=1.8, ls="--",
                dashes=(4, 2), alpha=0.85, label=gt_label, zorder=4)

    ax.set_title(f"K_true = {k_true}  (n=512, kmax=20)", fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("Exposure level k")
    ax.set_ylabel("P(adopt | exposure k)" if col == 0 else "")
    ax.legend(fontsize=7.5, loc="upper left")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig_synth_kernels_vs_truth.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
fig
```
